t: Count Pairs That Form a Complete Day I
o: Count pairs i < j with (hours[i] + hours[j]) % 24 == 0. Example 1: 12+12=24 ✓ and 24+24=48 ✓ → 2. Example 2: 72+48, 72+24, 48+24 all divisible by 24 → 3. With n ≤ 100, brute force works; bucketing by remainder mod 24 generalizes to large inputs.
k: Only remainders mod 24 matter: pair complements r with (24 − r) % 24.
Bucket counts by remainder; for each new element add the count of its complement seen so far (streaming avoids double counting).

a.i: Check all O(n²) pairs directly — at most 4950 pairs.
s: Count pairs whose sum is divisible by 24.

a.i: Stream through the array keeping counts of each remainder seen so far; for element with remainder r add cnt[(24 − r) % 24], then record r. This is O(n) and scales to the harder version with n up to 1e5.
s: For each hour: r = hour % 24; ans += cnt[(24 − r) % 24]; cnt[r]++.

w: Use the bucket method — it is just as short and scales. Pitfall: complement of 0 is 0 itself (and 12 pairs with 12); the streaming pattern handles self-pairing correctly without special cases. Watch overflow in Java/C++ if n were large (use long).
